Listen to this article Share Advertisement For Nigerian families seeking an international education for their children, the decision has often involved more than choosing a school. It can mean weighing the academic opportunities of studying abroad against the financial cost, distance from home and risk that children may build their futures elsewhere. Wellington College International Lagos wants to offer another option. Scheduled to open in September 2027 at Alaro City, the school will accommodate up to 1,500 students aged three to 18, following the English National Curriculum through to A-levels, according to the institution’s published plans. But its proposition goes beyond bringing a British curriculum to Nigeria. The school says it intends to combine international academic standards with Nigerian and African culture, technological readiness and the personal skills children will need in an increasingly unpredictable world. “We want to give these young people, as we do in all of our Wellington schools around the world, the best exam results, a global and service-minded outlook,” James Dahl, Master of Wellington College, said in an interview with BusinessDay. “But we want them to be really rooted in both their own communities, while being able to converse with, lead and follow, and engage with people from all the way around the world.” An education that goes beyond passing examinations The proposition addresses a wider challenge for Nigeria, where young people represent a substantial share of the population. The United Nations Population Fund estimates that 63 per cent of Nigerians are under 25, while those aged 10 to 24 account for 31.7 per cent of the population. The figures underscore the importance of preparing a large young population for changing economic opportunities. For Wellington College, that preparation means balancing academic achievement with the ability to adapt, solve problems, collaborate and exercise sound judgement. Artificial intelligence is central to this approach. Wellington College Education has established an Institute for Human Flourishing in the Age of AI, whose work Dahl said is being rolled out across its international schools. The aim, he explained, is to help students use AI to improve learning while understanding how to deploy the technology responsibly. Used strategically, AI could help personalise learning plans and free teachers to concentrate on mentoring, coaching and supporting students. The emphasis is not simply on technological fluency. Dahl argues that empathy, resilience, communication, and ethical judgement will remain important even as automation changes the workplace. This concern is supported by international evidence. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s PISA 2022 study found that, on average, only about half of students across participating countries and economies could easily judge the quality of information they encountered online. The finding highlights why digital education must develop critical thinking alongside the ability to use technology. The Nigerian dimension Wellington College’s model rests on the argument that international education should not come at the expense of local identity. Wellington College International Lagos is expected to incorporate Nigerian history, culture and heritage, alongside community service projects. Dahl described the approach as a partnership between international and local educational traditions, rather than the wholesale transplantation of a British school into another country. “The young people will mostly have two educational experiences: one which is local and one which is global,” he said. For parents considering overseas schooling, that combination could be attractive: students would have access to an internationally oriented curriculum while remaining immersed in the society in which many may eventually work, invest or build businesses. The school’s location is also part of its proposition. Developed in partnership with Rendeavour, Alaro City is planned as a mixed-use urban development with infrastructure, residential areas and commercial activity. Dahl said the partners’ long-term vision and emphasis on legacy helped persuade Wellington College to choose the site. He described the opportunity to establish the school as an educational anchor within the development as particularly compelling. Delivery begins in 2027 Wellington College International Lagos’ plans outline a co-educational day and boarding institution with academic, arts, sports, AI and entrepreneurship programmes. Dahl said Wellington does not intend to enter Nigeria on the assumption that it knows better than schools already operating in the country. Instead, he hopes its approach to innovation and professional exchange will contribute to wider discussions about how schools prepare children for the future. That ambition could give the institution influence beyond its own campus, particularly if its planned education forums bring local teachers and school leaders into meaningful exchange. Ultimately, Wellington College International Lagos is offering families a choice between leaving Nigeria for a global education and accessing an international model at home.
